Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

moral adjective

concerning right and wrong

also morally, moral question, moral philosophy, ethics, ethical

classical

Cic. Fat. 1: sed decet augentem linguam Latīnam nōmināre mōrālem (Lewis & Short)
Sen. Ep. 89.9; Quint. 12.2.10 (Lewis & Short)

mōrālis, mōrāle

adjective, third declension

moral, concerning conduct

Cicero made the word for Greek ἠθικός (Fat. 1), and Seneca and Quintilian took it up, mostly of the part of philosophy that deals with conduct. In plain speech Latin more often says dē mōribus, or names the duty in question (officium).

Other words

  • dē mōribus — about conduct, moral

    dē + ablative plural of mōs · also used · classical · Cic. Fat. 1: nōs eam partem philosophiae dē mōribus appellāre solēmus (Lewis & Short)

    The plain Latin: a moral question is a question about conduct (see morals).

Examples

  • quia pertinet ad mōrēs, quōs ἤθη Graecī vocant, nōs eam partem philosophiae dē mōribus appellāre solēmus; sed decet augentem linguam Latīnam nōmināre mōrālem

    because it concerns conduct, which the Greeks call ēthē, we usually call that part of philosophy “on conduct”; but in enriching the Latin language it is fitting to call it “moral”Cic. Fat. 1 (Lewis & Short)

  • philosophiae trēs partēs esse dīxērunt, mōrālem, nātūrālem, et ratiōnālem

    they said that philosophy has three parts, the moral, the natural and the rationalSen. Ep. 89.9 (Lewis & Short)

See also moral, morals, wrong.

SourcesLewis & Short: moralis · Lewis & Short: mos

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
